newsitem.title: FINLAND: Clinton leaves summit, U.S. claims major advances.
newsitem.headline: Clinton leaves summit, U.S. claims major advances.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton flew back to Washington on Friday after a summit with Russian President Boris Yeltsin with U.S. officials saying the two sides had made major progress on all issues under discussion.

Clinton hailed a series of agreements on arms control and integrating Russian into the world economy as well as a mutual understanding on NATO expansion, saying: "These are dramatic and very substantial results, and I'm very pleased with them.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright was even more enthusiastic.

"We were able to advance America's interest by cooperating on deep arms cuts, while building...a new Europe where NATO enlargement will take place and NATO-Russian cooperation will expand," Albright said.
"In other words, by pursuing our partnership with Russia, ensuring the enlargement of NATO and advancing the arms control agenda all at the same time, President Clinton made history in Helsinki"

On the enlargement of the North Atantic Treaty Organisation the two agreed to disagree, with Russia continuing to oppose the eastward expansion of the security alliance but agreeing to sign a document with NATO on their future relationship.

On economic matters, the United States set target dates for Russia joining the World Trade Organisation and the Paris Club of creditor countries. It also agreed to an enhanced Russian relationship with the Group of Seven leading industrial nations and to do more to support private investement in Russia.

And on arms control, the two said they would immediately embark on another round of nuclear arms reduction talks once Moscow has ratified the START-2 treaty, which would reduce their their nuclear arsenals to a maximumm of 3,500 each.

The framework for the new round of talks, called START-3, would bring their nuclear arsenals to a level of 2,000-2,500 strategic warheads per side by the end of 2007, about one fifth their level at the height of the Cold War.

Yeltsin also agreed to move quickly to seek ratification of START-2 by the Russian parliament, where it is opposed by many nationalists and communists. Russia and the United States also resolved a long-running dispute over misslie defence systems and reached an accord on chemical weapons.
The agreements allowed the U.S. negotiating team, as well as Yeltsin himself, to claim that the summit was a major success despite their continuing disagreement over NATO.

"On any issue we handled, we've been able to make a major breakthrough," Russian President Boris Yeltsin told reporters. "We didn't discuss small issues. We talked only about strategic issues and on all...were able to find an answer," he added.
Not all analysts viewed the agreements as an unqualified success.
Defence analyst John Steinbruner at Washington's Brookings Institution, argued the treatment of NATO's expansion did not resolve the underlying disagreement and might not be durable.
"The Russian government is admitting that they cannot prevent the expansion and I guess implicity saying there will not be any over-reaction," Steinbruner said.

"The underlying problem is that the Russian military have good reason to be seriously concerned by (NATO expansion)," he added. "This is not an equitable result...and you have to worry about the endurance and stability of a result that is not equitable."
"By forcing or inducing acquiescence by Russian political leaders, we've helped create faultlines between them and the Russian military leadership," Steinbruner said.

But Clinton, who left Helsinki late on Friday to return to Washington, said he himself was surprised by the amount of work that got done at the summit and singled out the agreements on START-2 and START-3 as especially significant.
